summary: Seeing Jesus pray, a disciple asks to be taught. Jesus gives Luke's form of the Lord's Prayer, then stories of a midnight friend and parental giving encourage bold persistence, culminating in the Father's gift of the Holy Spirit. After an exorcism, opponents accuse Jesus of using Beelzebul; Jesus answers with a divided kingdom, the stronger man, and God's finger. He warns that an emptied life needs new occupation, declares hearing and keeping God's word the true blessing, and gives Jonah and the queen of the South as witnesses against sign-seeking. Lamp and eye sayings examine perception. At a Pharisee's meal Jesus attacks cleansing without generosity, public honor, hidden contamination, burdensome legal expertise, and violence against prophets.
whyItMatters: Prayer forms dependence on daily provision, released debt, testing, and Spirit. Luke also refuses neutral emptiness: liberation must become a life inhabited by God's word and mercy. Religious expertise is judged by justice, generosity, humility, and whether it helps others enter.

context.author: The anonymous author, traditionally identified as Luke, collecting prayer, exorcism controversy, sign, perception, and meal-woe traditions
context.audience: Theophilus and a wider Greek-reading audience, here learning to pray and to distinguish liberation from religious performance
context.date: Commonly dated around AD 80–90, after AD 70; earlier dates in the 60s and later ones into the early second century are defended
context.setting: An unnamed place of prayer, houses and crowds, then a Pharisee's meal
context.literaryForm: Model prayer, household comparisons, controversy sayings, sign discourse, wisdom metaphors, and prophetic woes

outline.heading: A disciple asks; Jesus teaches the prayer
outline.note: A disciple asks for teaching on prayer; he gives words from 'Our Father in heaven' to 'deliver us from the evil one'.

outline.heading: Midnight persistence and the Father's Spirit gift
outline.note: A friend asks at midnight for three loaves and gets them by persistence; Jesus says keep asking, and the Father gives the Holy Spirit

outline.heading: Beelzebul accusation, divided rule, and stronger one
outline.note: Some say he casts out demons by Beelzebul; he says a divided kingdom falls and that whoever is not with him is against him

outline.heading: Returning spirit and hearing-kept blessing
outline.note: A spirit returns with seven worse ones; a woman praises the womb that bore him; he blesses those who hear and keep God's word

outline.heading: Jonah, southern queen, lamp, and eye
outline.note: This generation gets only Jonah's sign; the Queen of the South and Nineveh's men will condemn it; the eye is the body's lamp

outline.heading: Meal dispute and woes to Pharisees and lawyers
outline.note: Over dinner he says Pharisees clean the cup's outside, then pronounces woes on Pharisees and lawyers; scribes and Pharisees lie in wait for him

keyVerses.text: He said to them, “When you pray, say, ‘Our Father in heaven, may your name be kept holy. May your Kingdom come. May your will be done on earth, as it is in heaven.
keyVerses.why: Luke's prayer begins with God's name and reign before moving to daily communal need.

keyVerses.text: If you then, being evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him?”
keyVerses.why: Luke makes the Spirit the climactic good gift for which persistent disciples ask.

keyVerses.text: But he said, “On the contrary, blessed are those who hear the word of God, and keep it.”
keyVerses.why: Jesus relocates blessing from biological proximity to enacted hearing without, on one common reading, insulting his mother, who already models it (8:21).

questions.question: Why is Luke's Lord's Prayer shorter than Matthew's?
questions.answer: Early Greek witnesses differ here: the critical Greek text on this site has a more compact form, without ‘in heaven’ or ‘may your will be done,’ while the WEB displayed here includes the longer wording, close to Matthew 6:9-13. Jesus may have taught similar prayers more than once.

questions.question: What does ‘daily bread’ mean?
questions.answer: Epiousios is rare and debated: bread for the day, bread needed for existence, or bread for the coming day are leading senses. Luke's ‘day by day’ emphasizes recurring dependence. Eucharistic and future-banquet readings can enrich reception, but the immediate prayer includes ordinary material provision.

questions.question: Why does Luke say sins and then debts in the same line?
questions.answer: The prayer asks forgiveness of hamartiai, sins, ‘for we ourselves also forgive everyone who is indebted to us.’ Luke moves between moral failure and social-economic obligation. The metaphor explains forgiveness as release without claiming every loan is sinful or every injustice can be canceled without repair.

questions.question: Does the midnight story teach that God is reluctant and must be annoyed?
questions.answer: The difficult noun anaideia can mean shamelessness or bold persistence, on one reading describing the requester's refusal to accept social embarrassment. The comparison moves from a compromised human host to a generous Father: if even this household responds, how much more God. Prayer is encouraged, not divine stinginess.

questions.question: What is ‘God’s finger’?
questions.answer: It is scriptural shorthand for God's direct power, echoing the Exodus plagues and tablets. Jesus argues that if he expels demons by God's finger, God's kingdom has arrived. On one common reading, Luke's wording makes liberation a new-exodus sign rather than a technique of one rival exorcist.

questions.question: What does the returning unclean spirit warn about?
questions.answer: A swept, ordered, but empty house is vulnerable to worse reoccupation. On one common reading, removal of oppression must become positive allegiance, community, word-kept practice, and Spirit-filled life. The saying is not a formula blaming people when illness returns; it is a warning against treating liberation as morally neutral vacancy.

questions.question: Why is Jonah a sign in Luke?
questions.answer: Luke compares the Son of Man's relation to this generation with Jonah's presence to Nineveh and the queen's response to Solomon. Unlike Matthew, Luke does not explicitly say ‘three days and three nights’ here. The emphasis is on prophetic presence and outsiders who respond without receiving the demanded spectacle.

questions.question: Do the woes condemn all Pharisees or Jewish law?
questions.answer: No. Jesus is dining with a Pharisee and attacks specific performances: exterior cleansing with inward greed, tithing while neglecting justice and love, seeking honor, burdening others, and blocking knowledge. This is Jewish prophetic dispute about faithful practice; using it as an ethnic verdict repeats the hypocrisy it condemns.

glossary.def: Treated as holy and honored; the WEB here has ‘kept holy.’
Rare Greek adjective in ‘daily bread,’ with debated senses around present or coming provision.
Name for ‘the prince of the demons’ in the accusation against Jesus; one old explanation reads it as a contemptuous ‘lord of dung.’
Expert interpreter of Torah, not a modern courtroom attorney.
